ESE 3123 Study Pack

Thermo-Fluid Devices. One-shot notes, then every shortlisted past-paper topic (2019-2023) with full answers, slide figures and worked numericals. Your place, theme and text size are remembered on this device.

24-hour priority list

You answer 3 of 4 questions in each part, so each part has its own list. Study down both lists until the green pass line: about 3 h for Part A and 3 h for Part B, which leaves time for sleep and a last read of the one-shot notes. Alternate between parts (A block 1, B block 1, A block 2 …) so neither is left short. Chance: how often the topic came up, newer papers weigh more (2023 ×5, 2022 ×4, 2021 ×3, 2020 ×2, 2019 ×1). Covered: share of that part's past-paper marks you have studied once you finish the row.

Retake tip: read the Concept Primer first (30 minutes). Part A is mostly pumps and flow meters: the venturi/Pitot numericals (A4), affinity laws (A7) and the reciprocating pump numerical (A8) are short and come every year, and each has a calculator. In Part B the heat exchanger numericals (B5, B6) are the safest marks; the normal-shock calculator (B3) gives every downstream property in one go. Leave dimensional analysis (A3) and nozzle derivations (B2) for last.

One-shot notes: ESE 3123 Thermo-Fluid Devices

Pipe flow (A1)

Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν: laminar < 2300, transition 2300-4000, turbulent > 4000. Entrance length Lh ≈ 0.05ReD (laminar), 10D (turbulent); beyond it the flow is fully developed.

Darcy-Weisbach hL = f(L/D)(V2/2g); laminar f = 64/Re; turbulent from Moody/Colebrook (f depends on Re and ε/D). Minor loss h = K V2/2g.

Laminar profile: u = umax(1 − r2/R2), Vavg = umax/2, ΔP = 32μLV/D2 (Hagen-Poiseuille). Turbulent profile is flatter.

Pipe numericals (A2)

Steps: Re → f → hL → ΔP = ρghL → W = QΔP.

2019 2b: Re 1777, f 0.036, hL 4.46 m, ΔP 43.7 kPa, W 0.28 W. 2023 6d: Re 1836, ΔP 188.2 kPa, hL 19.2 m, W 0.71 W.

Series: same Q, hL add. Parallel: same hL, Q add. 2021 1c ratio 45.7. 3-inch pipe: 10S ID 3.260 in; sch 40 ID 3.068 in; XXS ID 2.300 in.

Dimensional analysis (A3)

Fundamental dimensions M, L, T (θ). Homogeneity: every term has the same dimensions. Rayleigh: write Q = kAaBb..., equate powers of M, L, T.

Buckingham π: n variables, m dimensions ⇒ (n − m) π groups; choose m repeating variables (geometric, kinematic, dynamic: usually D, V, ρ), each π = DaVbρcX. Drag gives F/(ρV2D2) = f(Re).

Flow meters (A4)

Venturi: Q = Cda1a2√(2gh)/√(a12 − a22), h = x(Sm/S − 1); Cd 0.95-0.99. Orifice same with Cd 0.6-0.65 (vena contracta). Pitot V = Cv√(2gh).

Rotameter: float rises in tapered tube until weight = drag + buoyancy (variable area). Turbine meter: rotor speed ∝ Q.

Venturi Q 125.8 L/s. Pitot 2020: h 2.451 m, V 6.93 m/s; 2022: 2.328 m, 6.76 m/s. Air venturi 2019 6d: 3.12 kg/s (3.25 if incompressible).

Centrifugal pump (A5)

Parts: impeller, casing (volute, vortex, diffuser), suction pipe with foot valve and strainer, delivery pipe with valve. Converts mechanical energy into pressure energy by centrifugal action.

Work per unit weight = Vw2u2/g (radial entry, Vw1 = 0). Manometric head Hm = hs + hd + hfs + hfd + Vd2/2g.

ηmano = gHm/(Vw2u2); ηmech = impeller power/shaft power; ηo = ρgQHm/P.

Pump performance (A6)

Curves: H, P, η vs Q at constant N; BEP at peak η. Affinity: Q ∝ ND3, H ∝ N2D2, P ∝ N3D5.

Ns = N√Q/H3/4 (per stage, per eye). Cavitation: local P < Pvap ⇒ bubbles collapse, pitting, noise, drop of H and η. NPSHA = (Patm − Pv)/ρg − hs − hfs ≥ NPSHR.

Priming: fill suction pipe and casing with liquid before starting (air gives too little head).

Pump numericals (A7)

Series: H adds. 2020 3d: 31.9 m per pump ⇒ 3.14 ⇒ 4 pumps. Multistage: n = H/Hstage; 2021 3d: Ns 322, 18.8 m/stage, 10 stages, D 58.7 cm. 2022 4d: Ns 672.7, 19 stages, D 36.7 cm (alt. 10 stages, 35.8 cm).

Affinity: 2023 3d: 866 rpm, 92.4 gpm, 9.24 hp. 2019 7d: 1072 rpm, 122.5 gpm, 14.7 hp.

Reciprocating pump (A8)

Qth = ALN/60 (single acting), 2ALN/60 (double). Slip = Qth − Qact; % slip = (1 − Cd)100; negative slip when long suction, high speed. P = ρgQth(hs + hd).

2020 2b: Cd 0.960, slip 3.96%, P 4.21 kW. 2021 4d: slip −1.86%, Cd 1.019, P 7.38 kW. 2023 4d: slip 8.33%, Cd 0.917. 2019 8c: N 83.2 rpm, H 117.1 m, P 130.2 kW.

Plunger: piston-type, high pressure. Diaphragm: flexible membrane, leak-free, slurries/chemicals.

Compressors and fans (A9)

Fan (pressure ratio < 1.1), blower (1.1-1.2), compressor (> 1.2). Reciprocating (high P, low Q), rotary screw/vane, centrifugal and axial (large Q).

Isothermal efficiency = isothermal work/actual work; FD fan pushes air into the furnace, ID fan pulls gas out through the stack.

Compressible basics (B1)

Ma = V/c; incompressible < 0.3, subsonic < 1, sonic = 1, transonic 0.8-1.2, supersonic 1-5, hypersonic > 5.

c = √(K/ρ) = √(kRT); air 300 K: 347 m/s. T0/T = 1 + (k − 1)Ma2/2; P0/P = (T0/T)k/(k−1). Adiabatic Bernoulli: [k/(k−1)]p/ρg + V2/2g + z = C.

Air critical: T*/T0 0.8333, P*/P0 0.5283, ρ*/ρ0 0.6339. 2021 5d: 324.8 m/s vs 291.4 m/s incompressible.

Nozzles (B2)

dA/A = (Ma2 − 1)dV/V: subsonic nozzle converges, supersonic nozzle diverges, Ma = 1 only at the throat.

ṁmax = A*P0√(k/RT0)[2/(k + 1)](k+1)/2(k−1) = 0.6847A*P0/√(RT0) air. Back pressure below P* ⇒ choked, no further rise in ṁ.

2022 5c: T* 301 K, P* 118 kPa, A*/A1 0.629. 2020 4c CO2: V 164.9, ρ 13.9, A 13.1 cm2, Ma 0.494. 2023 1d: ṁ 2.86 kg/s, Ve 845 m/s, Ae 33.75 cm2. 2019 5d: 6.78 and 7.11 kg/s.

Shocks (B3)

Normal shock: supersonic → subsonic, P, T, ρ, s up, P0 down, T0 same. Oblique: inclined, flow turned, weaker.

Ma22 = (Ma12 + 5)/(7Ma12 − 1) (air); P2/P1 = (1 + kMa12)/(1 + kMa22) (Rayleigh line). Shock states = Rayleigh ∩ Fanno.

Ma 2: Ma2 0.577, P ratio 4.5, T ratio 1.6875. Ma 2.5: 0.513, 7.125, 2.1375. Ma 2.2: 0.547, 5.48, 1.857.

HX fundamentals (B4)

Recuperator, regenerator, direct contact; parallel, counter, cross flow; double pipe, shell-and-tube, plate, compact.

1/UA = 1/hiAi + Rf,i/Ai + ln(Do/Di)/2πkL + Rf,o/Ao + 1/hoAo; thin clean: U = 1/(1/hi + 1/ho). Rf = 1/Udirty − 1/Uclean.

Q = UAΔTlm, ΔTlm = (ΔT1 − ΔT2)/ln(ΔT1/ΔT2). Counter flow: bigger LMTD, Tc,o can exceed Th,o.

LMTD numericals (B5)

Energy balance first, then ΔTlm, A = Q/UΔTlm, L = A/πD.

2020 5c: 301 kW, LMTD 92.0, L 108.5 m. 2020 6b: 28.4 m2. 2022 7c: 15.8 m2. 2021 7c: U 43.7, L 92.5 m. 2023 7c: L 0.968 m; Rf 9.5×10−4. 2019 4c: U 37.7, L 66.6 m. 2023 8c: Tw,o 18.5 °C, UA 785 W/K, L 5.0 m.

Effectiveness-NTU (B6)

ε = Q/[Cmin(Th,i − Tc,i)]; NTU = UA/Cmin; Cr = Cmin/Cmax.

Parallel: ε = [1 − e−NTU(1+Cr)]/(1 + Cr). Counter: ε = [1 − e−NTU(1−Cr)]/[1 − Cre−NTU(1−Cr)]; NTU = [1/(Cr − 1)]ln[(ε − 1)/(εCr − 1)].

2021 8c: ṁw 0.403 kg/s, ε 0.75, NTU 2.35, A 2.18 m2. 2022 8d: NTU 2.50, ε 0.8325, Q 133.3 kW, Tc,o 86.6 °C.

Definitions to know by heart

Cavitation, priming, NPSH, specific speed (speed of a geometrically similar pump giving 1 m3/s against 1 m), slip, manometric efficiency, vena contracta, Cd, Mach number, stagnation property, choking, shock wave, fouling factor, effectiveness, NTU, heat capacity rate.

Sketches to practise

1 Reynolds regimes and Moody chart; 2 entrance region; 3 laminar vs turbulent profile; 4 venturimeter; 5 orifice with vena contracta; 6 Pitot tube; 7 rotameter; 8 centrifugal pump and casings; 9 velocity triangles; 10 pump curves; 11 NPSH/suction; 12 reciprocating pump and indicator diagram; 13 C-D nozzle pressure plot; 14 back-pressure effect; 15 normal shock and Rayleigh-Fanno; 16 parallel vs counter temperature profiles; 17 ε-NTU chart.

LEARN IT FROM ZERO
Flow meters, from zero

All obstruction meters (venturi, orifice, nozzle) use one idea: squeeze the flow, it speeds up, its pressure drops (Bernoulli). Measure the pressure drop with a manometer and you know the speed.

A differential manometer reading x of a heavy liquid (mercury, Sh) under a lighter one (So) is a head of flowing liquid h = x(Sh/So − 1). Then Bernoulli plus continuity give Q = Cda1a2√(2gh)/√(a1² − a2²). Cd corrects for friction and the vena contracta: venturi 0.95–0.99 (smooth, little loss), nozzle about 0.95, orifice about 0.6 (cheap but big loss).

A Pitot tube faces the flow; the fluid stops at its tip, so the extra (stagnation) head is V²/2g, giving V = Cv√(2gh).

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: how flow meters work

Put an obstruction in the pipe: the area falls, so by continuity (Q = AV) the velocity rises, and by Bernoulli the pressure falls. A manometer reads the pressure drop; from it we get the velocity and the flow rate. Real fluids lose some energy, so the ideal flow is multiplied by a coefficient of discharge Cd < 1.

Differential U-tube manometer with a heavier liquid (mercury, Sh = 13.6) under a flowing liquid So: pressure head difference h = x(Sh/So − 1) metres of the flowing liquid, x = difference in mercury levels.

Common flow-rate measuring instruments (2022 2b)
  • Obstruction (differential-pressure) meters: venturimeter, orifice meter, flow nozzle
  • Velocity probes: Pitot tube, Pitot-static tube (point velocity), hot-wire anemometer
  • Variable area meter: rotameter
  • Turbine and paddle-wheel meters; positive-displacement (nutating disc) meters
  • Electromagnetic, ultrasonic (Doppler/transit-time), vortex-shedding and Coriolis (mass) meters
Venturimeter: description and discharge (2020 1b, 2019 6c)

A venturimeter measures the discharge through a pipe. It has a short converging cone (about 20°), a cylindrical throat (d/D = 0.4-0.7) and a long diverging cone (5-7°, long so that the flow does not separate and most of the pressure is recovered). Pressure taps at the inlet (1) and throat (2) go to a differential manometer. (Hydraulic diameter Dh = 4A/p: see A1.)

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Bernoulli 1 → 2 (horizontal, z1 = z2): p1/ρg + V12/2g = p2/ρg + V22/2gIdeal flow.
h = (p1 − p2)/ρg = (V22 − V12)/2gh = venturi head, from the manometer.
Continuity: A1V1 = A2V2 ⇒ V1 = V2A2/A1
2gh = V22(1 − A22/A12) ⇒ V2 = A1√(2gh)/√(A12 − A22)
Qth = A2V2 = A1A2√(2gh)/√(A12 − A22)Theoretical discharge.
Qact = CdA1A2√(2gh)/√(A12 − A22), Cd = 0.96-0.99Friction makes the actual flow a little smaller.
Nozzle meter (2022 2c)

A flow nozzle is a smooth converging nozzle with a short cylindrical throat placed in the pipe; it has no long diverging cone (cheaper and shorter than a venturi, used for high-pressure steam). Bernoulli between the pipe (1) and the nozzle throat (2) and continuity give exactly the venturi result: Q = CdA1A2√(2gh)/√(A12 − A22) with Cd = 0.95-0.98 (write the same six steps as above with A2 = nozzle throat area).

Orifice meter (2019 3b, 2023 5b)

An orifice meter is a thin plate with a sharp-edged circular hole (diameter about 0.5D) clamped between pipe flanges. Taps: one about 1.5-2D upstream (section 1), one at the vena contracta (section 2, about D/2 downstream). Cheap and compact, but the sudden expansion after the jet wastes much energy.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Bernoulli 1 → 2: (p1 − p2)/ρg + (z1 − z2) = h = (V22 − V12)/2g ⇒ V2 = √(2gh + V12)Section 2 is at the vena contracta.
Jet area A2 = CcAo; continuity A1V1 = A2V2 ⇒ V1 = (AoCc/A1)V2Cc = coefficient of contraction.
V22[1 − (Ao/A1)2Cc2] = 2gh ⇒ V2 = √(2gh)/√(1 − (Ao/A1)2Cc2)
Q = A2V2 = AoCc√(2gh)/√(1 − (Ao/A1)2Cc2)Contains the unknown Cc.
Define Cd = Cc√(1 − (Ao/A1)2)/√(1 − (Ao/A1)2Cc2)Lumps contraction and friction (include Cv for losses).
Q = CdAoA1√(2gh)/√(A12 − Ao2), Cd ≈ 0.61-0.65Same form as the venturi with Ao in place of the throat area.
Vena contracta (2021 2c)

The vena contracta is the section of a jet just downstream of an orifice (about 0.5Do from the plate) where the jet area is the smallest, the velocity the largest and the pressure the lowest. It forms because the streamlines converge towards the hole and, by inertia, keep converging for a short distance after it instead of turning sharply. Cc = Ac/Ao ≈ 0.61-0.69.

Venturimeter vs orifice meter (2022 2b) and relative accuracy (2023 5c)
FeatureVenturimeterNozzle meterOrifice meter
Constructionconverging cone, throat, long diverging coneshort smooth converging nozzlethin plate with a sharp-edged hole
Cd0.96-0.990.95-0.980.61-0.65
Permanent pressure losslow (10-15% of Δp)moderate (40-60%)high (60-80%)
Accuracyhighest (±0.5-1%), Cd well known and steadygood (±1-2%)lowest (±1-3%); edge wear and deposits change Cd
Space and costlong, costlymediumcompact, cheapest, easy to change
Uselarge water and process lines where pumping cost mattershigh-pressure steam linesgeneral/lab use, gas lines, where loss is acceptable

Relative accuracy: venturi > nozzle > orifice. The smooth venturi has almost no contraction or separation, so its Cd is close to 1 and changes little with Re; the orifice has a strong vena contracta and eddies, so its Cd is low and depends on Re, edge sharpness and tap position.

Hydraulic coefficients (2021 2b)
CoefficientDefinitionTypical value
Coefficient of contraction Ccarea of jet at vena contracta / area of orifice0.61-0.69
Coefficient of velocity Cvactual velocity at vena contracta / theoretical velocity √(2gH)0.95-0.99
Coefficient of discharge Cdactual discharge / theoretical discharge = Cc × Cv0.61-0.65
Coefficient of resistance Crhead lost in the orifice / head remaining in the jet = 1/Cv2 − 1small
Pitot tube: velocity at a point (2021 2b, 2019 3a)

A Pitot tube is a small bent tube with its open end facing the flow. At the tip the fluid is brought to rest (stagnation point), so the kinetic energy changes into pressure energy and the liquid in the tube rises above the free surface by h. Measuring h gives the velocity at that point. Arrangements: Pitot tube with a vertical piezometer; Pitot-static tube (two concentric tubes: stagnation hole at the nose and static holes on the side) connected to a differential U-tube manometer, used in pipes and on aircraft.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Point 1 upstream (velocity V1, pressure head H below the surface); point 2 at the tip (V2 = 0, pressure head H + h)Same streamline, same level.
p1/ρg + V12/2g = p2/ρg ⇒ H + V12/2g = H + hBernoulli, z1 = z2.
V1 = √(2gh) (theoretical)Dynamic head h = V2/2g.
Vact = Cv√(2gh), Cv ≈ 0.98Coefficient of the Pitot tube; with a U-tube h = x(Sh/So − 1).
Rotameter (2019 3c)

A rotameter is a variable-area flow meter: a vertical tapered transparent tube (wider at the top) containing a float. The fluid enters at the bottom and flows up through the annular gap between float and tube. The float rises until the upward forces (drag of the fluid + buoyancy) balance its weight. As it rises the annular area grows, so the velocity and drag in the gap fall; for every flow rate there is one balance height. The flow rate is read directly from the scale on the tube at the top edge of the float. Simple, direct reading, low pressure loss, good for small gas and liquid flows (laboratories, oxygen and anaesthesia lines); must be vertical, glass is fragile, accuracy only ±2-5%.

Numerical 1: venturimeter 30 cm × 15 cm, 20 cm of mercury (2022 2d, 2023 5d)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
A1 = (π/4)(0.30)2 = 0.07069 m2; A2 = (π/4)(0.15)2 = 0.01767 m2
h = x(Sh/So − 1) = 0.20(13.6/1 − 1) = 2.52 m of waterMercury under water.
Q = CdA1A2√(2gh)/√(A12 − A22) = 0.98 × 0.07069 × 0.01767 × √(2 × 9.81 × 2.52)/√(0.070692 − 0.017672)
Q = 0.1258 m3/s = 125.8 L/sBansal Problem 6.10 (125.76 L/s).
Numerical 2: speed of a submarine by Pitot tube (2020 1c: 200 mm; 2022 1c “Titan”: 190 mm)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
h = x(SHg/Ssea − 1) = 0.200(13.6/1.026 − 1) = 2.451 m of sea waterThe 15 m depth cancels: it adds equally to both limbs.
V = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.81 × 2.451) = 6.93 m/s = 24.96 km/h2020 answer (take Cv = 1).
2022: h = 0.190(13.6/1.026 − 1) = 2.328 m; V = √(2 × 9.81 × 2.328) = 6.76 m/s = 24.3 km/hRelative velocity of water past the submarine = speed of the submarine.
Numerical 3: mass flow of air through a venturimeter (2019 6d)

Given: D1 = 0.40 m, D2 = 0.15 m, p1 = 137 kPa, T1 = 288.15 K, p2 = 127 kPa, R = 287, γ = 1.4. Air is compressible, so use the adiabatic (isentropic) energy equation instead of Bernoulli.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
ρ1 = p1/RT1 = 137,000/(287 × 288.15) = 1.657 kg/m3Ideal gas.
ρ2 = ρ1(p2/p1)1/γ = 1.657(127/137)0.714 = 1.569 kg/m3; T2 = 282.0 Kp/ργ = constant.
Energy: V22/2 − V12/2 = [γ/(γ − 1)](p1/ρ1 − p2/ρ2) = 3.5(82,699 − 80,927) = 6,201 J/kgAdiabatic Bernoulli (see B1).
Continuity: ρ1A1V1 = ρ2A2V2 ⇒ V1 = (1.569 × 0.01767)/(1.657 × 0.1257) V2 = 0.1332V2A1 = 0.1257, A2 = 0.01767 m2.
V22(1 − 0.13322) = 2 × 6,201 ⇒ V2 = 112.4 m/s
ṁ = ρ2A2V2 = 1.569 × 0.01767 × 112.4 = 3.12 kg/sTreating the air as incompressible would give 3.25 kg/s, 4% high.

★ REMEMBER IT
  • Affinity laws (same pump, speed changes): Q ∝ N, H ∝ N², P ∝ N³ (with diameter: Q ∝ ND³, H ∝ N²D², P ∝ N³D5). Remember "1, 2, 3".
  • Specific speed Ns = N√Q/H3/4: speed of a geometrically similar pump that delivers 1 m³/s against 1 m. Low Ns = radial (high head), high Ns = axial (high flow).
  • Cavitation: suction pressure falls below vapour pressure → bubbles form → they collapse in the high-pressure zone → pitting, noise, vibration, lower head. Avoid it by keeping NPSHavailable > NPSHrequired.
  • Priming: fill the suction pipe and casing with liquid first. Air is ~800 times lighter, so the impeller would make only a tiny head in air and could not lift water.
Before you start: reading a pump’s behaviour

A pump never runs at just one point. When the valve opens wider, Q rises and the head the pump can give falls. The manufacturer’s test results, plotted as curves, show how head, power and efficiency change with flow and speed. Two tools let us predict new conditions without new tests: the affinity laws (same pump, new speed or diameter) and the specific speed (which type of pump suits a duty).

Pumps can only push liquid, never vapour. If the pressure at the impeller eye falls below the vapour pressure, the liquid boils locally: that is cavitation, and NPSH is the margin that prevents it.

Characteristic curves and their significance (2020 3a, 2022 4b, 2023 3a)

Significance: characteristic curves show the actual behaviour of a pump found by tests: the head, power and efficiency it gives at each discharge and speed. They are used to choose a pump for a duty, to find its best efficiency point (BEP), to predict how it will behave at other speeds, and to find the operating point with a given pipe system.

  • Main characteristic curves: the speed N is kept constant at several values (N1, N2, N3), and Hm, shaft power P and efficiency are plotted against Q for each speed (by throttling the delivery valve). Hm falls as Q rises; higher N gives higher curves.
  • Operating characteristic curves: at the design speed only, Hm, P and η are plotted against Q on one graph. η rises to a maximum at the design point (BEP) and then falls; P rises with Q (it is not zero at Q = 0 because of losses); Hm is highest at shut-off (Q = 0).
  • Constant-efficiency (iso-efficiency, Muschel) curves: from the main curves, points of equal η are joined on the H-Q plane; they show the range of speed and flow for good efficiency.
  • Operating point: the system curve H = Hstatic + KQ2 (pipe losses) crosses the pump H-Q curve at the point where the pump will run.

Fans, compressors and blowers (2020 3a): see the table in A9: fan specific ratio up to 1.11, blower 1.11-1.20, compressor above 1.20.

Affinity laws (2023 3a, 2019 7b)

For geometrically similar pumps (or the same pump) running at similar operating points (same efficiency), the flow coefficient Q/ND3, head coefficient gH/N2D2 and power coefficient P/ρN3D5 stay constant. Hence:

ChangeFlowHeadPower
speed N (same D)Q2/Q1 = N2/N1H2/H1 = (N2/N1)2P2/P1 = (N2/N1)3
impeller diameter D (same N)∝ D (trimmed impeller) or D3 (similar pumps)∝ D2∝ D3 (trimmed) or D5

When engineers use them: to predict the new flow, head and power when the motor speed is changed (variable-speed drives); to find the speed needed when the system head changes (new heat exchanger, longer pipe); to trim an impeller to a new duty; to scale a model test to a prototype; and to draw new H-Q curves at other speeds. Doubling the speed doubles Q, quadruples H and needs 8 times the power.

Specific speed: definition and derivation (2020 3b, 2022 4a)

Specific speed Ns of a centrifugal pump is the speed of a geometrically similar pump that would deliver 1 m3/s against a head of 1 m. It has no direct physical meaning but is the same for all similar pumps, so it tells the type of impeller: radial (low Ns, 10-80), mixed flow (80-160), axial (above 160, SI units with Q in m3/s).

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Q = (area) × (velocity of flow) = πDB VfD = impeller diameter, B = width.
B ∝ D (similar pumps) ⇒ Q ∝ D2Vf
Tangential velocity u = πDN/60 ∝ DN, and u ∝ Vf ∝ √H (u = Ku√(2gH))Velocities scale with √(head).
⇒ D ∝ √H/N and Vf ∝ √H
Q ∝ (√H/N)2√H = H3/2/N2 ⇒ Q = K H3/2/N2K = constant for similar pumps.
Definition: H = 1 m and Q = 1 m3/s when N = Ns ⇒ 1 = K/Ns2, K = Ns2
Q = Ns2H3/2/N2 ⇒ Ns = N√Q/Hm3/4Q at best efficiency; Hm per stage.

Dependence on Hm and Q (2022 4a): the result shows that, for a given speed, Ns rises as √Q and falls as Hm3/4: high-head, low-flow duties need low-Ns radial pumps; low-head, high-flow duties need high-Ns axial (propeller) pumps.

Cavitation and NPSH (2020 3c, 2022 4c, 2023 4a, 2019 8a)

Cavitation is the formation of vapour bubbles in a flowing liquid where the local absolute pressure falls below the vapour pressure at that temperature, followed by the sudden collapse of these bubbles when they are carried into a region of higher pressure. Where: at the eye and inlet of the vanes of a centrifugal pump (lowest pressure), at the outlet of reaction turbines (draft tube), on ship propellers and in valves. Why: high suction lift, high liquid temperature (higher pv), high speed or flow beyond the BEP (best efficiency point), long or narrow suction pipe (friction), low atmospheric pressure at altitude, clogged strainer.

Effects: collapsing bubbles produce very high local pressures (up to thousands of bar) that hammer the metal: pitting and erosion of impeller vanes, noise and vibration, and a sudden fall in head, discharge and efficiency.

Precautions: keep the pressure everywhere above pv, i.e. NPSHA > NPSHR: low suction lift (place the pump near or below the liquid level), short, large-diameter suction pipe with few bends, avoid hot liquid, do not exceed the design speed/flow, keep strainers clean, use cavitation-resistant materials (stainless steel, aluminium bronze).

NPSH (net positive suction head) is the total head at the pump suction above the vapour pressure head: NPSH = ps/ρg + Vs2/2g − pv/ρg = patm/ρg − pv/ρg − hs − hfs. NPSHA (available) is fixed by the system; NPSHR (required) is given by the manufacturer for the pump at each flow. Significance: it is the criterion for cavitation-free operation, used to fix the pump elevation and the suction pipe; the pump industry specifies NPSHR on every pump curve, and a margin NPSHA ≥ NPSHR + 0.5-1 m is kept. Thoma’s cavitation factor σ = NPSH/Hm; cavitation starts when σ < σc.

Priming (2021 4a), and running the impeller in air (2020 2c)

Priming is the filling of the suction pipe, the casing and the part of the delivery pipe up to the delivery valve with the liquid to be pumped, so that all air (or vapour) is removed before starting the pump. Methods: filling from an overhead tank or by hand through a funnel (foot valve holds it), using a vacuum pump, or self-priming designs.

Why it is necessary (and what happens in air): the head developed by the impeller, H = Vw2u2/g, depends only on the velocities, not on the fluid. The pressure it produces is ρgH, which is proportional to the density of the fluid in the impeller. Air is about 800 times lighter than water (1.2 vs 1000 kg/m3), so an impeller running in air produces only about 1/800 of the pressure: e.g. a pump designed for 40 m of water makes only 40/800 = 0.05 m (5 cm) of water pressure difference. That cannot lift water up the suction pipe (needs several metres), so no liquid is delivered: the pump simply churns the air. Running dry also overheats and damages the seals, wearing rings and bearings because there is no liquid to cool and lubricate them. Hence the pump must be primed.

Maximum suction height (2021 4b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Bernoulli from the sump surface (1) to the pump inlet (2), sump as datum: patm/ρg + 0 + 0 = ps/ρg + Vs2/2g + hs + hfshs = suction height, hfs = friction loss in the suction pipe.
ps/ρg = patm/ρg − (hs + hfs + Vs2/2g)Suction pressure falls as hs rises.
No cavitation: ps/ρg ≥ pv/ρg (strictly + NPSHR)Limit.
hs,max = (patm − pv)/ρg − hfs − Vs2/2g (− NPSHR)Maximum suction height.
For cold water at sea level: 10.3 − 0.24 = about 10 m in theory; in practice 6-7 mNever above 10.3 m.

Memory trick: Affinity laws “1-2-3”: Q ∝ N1, H ∝ N2, P ∝ N3. Specific speed: “N root Q over H to the three-quarters”.

UNDERSTAND Read this to understand; you do not need to write it

A reciprocating pump is a syringe on a crank: the piston pulls liquid in through the suction valve, then pushes it out through the delivery valve. Theoretical flow is the swept volume times strokes: Qth = ALN/60 (double-acting × 2, three-throw × 3). Real flow is a little less because valves leak and close late: slip = Qth − Qact. If a long delivery pipe's momentum keeps the delivery valve open, Qact > Qth: negative slip.

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: positive-displacement pumps

A reciprocating pump traps a fixed volume of liquid in a cylinder and pushes it out with a piston, like a syringe. Each stroke delivers a known volume, so the theoretical discharge is just (swept volume) × (strokes per second). It can make very high pressure but gives a small, pulsating flow.

Some liquid leaks back through the valves before they close, so the actual discharge is a little less: the difference is slip.

Working principle of a reciprocating pump (2022 3a, 2023 4c, 2019 8b)

Hydraulic machines: see A5. A reciprocating pump is a positive-displacement pump in which a piston or plunger moves to and fro in a close-fitting cylinder. Main parts: cylinder with piston, piston rod, connecting rod and crank (driven by a motor), suction pipe with suction (non-return) valve, delivery pipe with delivery (non-return) valve, strainer.

  1. Suction stroke: the crank turns from inner dead centre (θ = 0) to outer dead centre (θ = 180°); the piston moves away from the valves, the volume increases and a partial vacuum forms in the cylinder. Atmospheric pressure on the sump pushes liquid up the suction pipe, opens the suction valve and fills the cylinder; the delivery valve stays closed.
  2. Delivery stroke: the crank turns from 180° to 360°; the piston moves back towards the valves and the pressure rises. The suction valve closes and the delivery valve opens; the liquid is forced up the delivery pipe.
  3. The cycle repeats, so the delivery is intermittent (pulsating). Air vessels on the suction and delivery pipes smooth the flow and save power.
Slip, percentage slip and negative slip (2023 4c, 2019 8b, 2020 2a)

Qth = ALN/60 (single acting)   Qth = 2ALN/60 (double acting)   Slip = Qth − Qact   % slip = (Qth − Qact)/Qth × 100 = (1 − Cd) × 100

Slip is the difference between the theoretical and actual discharge, caused by leakage past the piston and valves and by the delay in closing the valves; Cd = Qact/Qth (volumetric efficiency, 0.95-0.98); slip is about 2% in a good pump. Negative slip occurs when Qact > Qth (Cd > 1). Reason: with a long suction pipe, short delivery pipe and high speed, the inertia (momentum) of the long column of liquid in the suction pipe is large compared with the pressure on the delivery side; near the end of the suction stroke the moving liquid keeps flowing and pushes open the delivery valve before the delivery stroke starts. Some liquid goes straight to the delivery pipe, so more is delivered than the swept volume.

Classification; centrifugal vs reciprocating (2021 4c)
  • According to the sides of the piston in contact with water: single-acting (one side, one suction and one delivery pipe) and double-acting (both sides, two suction and two delivery valves; twice the discharge).
  • According to the number of cylinders: single-cylinder, double-cylinder (two-throw) and triple-cylinder (three-throw, cranks 120° apart, smoother flow).
  • According to the element: piston pump, plunger pump, diaphragm pump; with or without air vessels.
Centrifugal pumpReciprocating pump
rotodynamic: energy from a rotating impellerpositive displacement: piston pushes trapped liquid
continuous, steady flowintermittent, pulsating flow
large discharge, small to medium headsmall discharge, high head
handles viscous, dirty liquids, slurriesclean, low-viscosity liquids only (valves clog)
high speed, direct coupled to a motor; compact, low costlow speed, belt or gear drive; needs 6-7 times the floor area, high cost
needs primingself-priming
simple, few parts, low maintenance; uniform torquecomplex (valves, crank); high maintenance; uneven torque
efficiency high at design pointefficiency can be low at low head (about 40%)
Plunger pumps vs diaphragm pumps (2023 4b)
Plunger pumpDiaphragm pump
Principlesolid plunger moves through a stationary packing/seal in the cylinderflexible diaphragm (rubber, thermoplastic, PTFE) flexed by a rod, hydraulic oil or air (AODD) changes the chamber volume
Advantagesvery high pressures (70-2000 bar); pressure can change without changing the flow; high efficiency; accurate meteringliquid never touches moving parts or seals, so no leakage; handles slurries (up to 75% solids), abrasive, corrosive and viscous liquids; self-priming, can run dry; good suction lift
Disadvantagespulsating flow; packing wears and leaks; not for abrasive or very acidic liquids; heavy, high maintenancelimited pressure and flow; diaphragm fatigues and must be replaced; pulsating; air-operated types use much compressed air
Applicationshigh-pressure cleaning, oil-well service, hydraulic testing, boiler feed, chemical injection, sludgechemical dosing, paints, mine and site dewatering, food and pharma transfer, slurries, fuel pumps

Before you start: how to solve multistage pump problems

Similar pumps have the same specific speed Ns = N√Q/H3/4, where H is the head of one stage. In a multistage pump the stages are in series: the same Q goes through each and the heads add. So: (1) find Ns from the given pump, (2) find the head per stage of the new pump from Ns, (3) number of stages = total head / head per stage (round up), (4) diameter from the head coefficient √H/(DN) = constant.

The efficiency given in these questions is not needed (it would only be used for power).

Hm = 13.424/3 = 31.9 m
Number of pumps = 100/31.9 = 3.14Pumps in series share the total head.
4 pumps in series (3 would give only 96 m); each then works at 25 mRound up.

★ REMEMBER IT
  • Pump vs turbine: a pump puts energy into the liquid (mechanical → pressure head); a turbine takes it out.
  • Centrifugal pump parts: I-C-S-D: Impeller (curved vanes, spins the liquid), Casing (volute or with guide blades turns velocity into pressure), Suction pipe with foot valve and strainer, Delivery pipe with valve.
  • Efficiencies chain: shaft power → (mechanical η) → power given to liquid by impeller → (manometric η = gHm/Vw2u2) → useful power ρgQHm. Overall ηo = ηmano × ηmech.
  • Work done per unit weight = Vw2u2/g (radial entry, Vw1 = 0).
Before you start: what a pump does

A hydraulic machine converts energy between a liquid and a machine. A turbine takes hydraulic energy from water and gives mechanical energy (shaft work); a pump takes mechanical energy from a motor and gives hydraulic energy (pressure) to a liquid, so that it can be lifted to a height or pushed through pipes.

In a centrifugal pump a spinning impeller whirls the liquid (a forced vortex). The centrifugal action throws the liquid outward at high speed; the casing then slows it down and turns the velocity into pressure. Head is measured in metres of liquid: H = pressure/ρg.

Hydraulic machines; turbine vs pump (2021 3a)

Hydraulic machines are machines that convert hydraulic energy (energy of a liquid) into mechanical energy (turbines) or mechanical energy into hydraulic energy (pumps). Examples: Pelton, Francis and Kaplan turbines; centrifugal and reciprocating pumps.

TurbinePump
converts hydraulic energy of water into mechanical (shaft) energyconverts mechanical energy into hydraulic (pressure) energy of the liquid
water flows from high head to low head; drives a generatorliquid is raised from low head to high head; driven by a motor
flow (reaction turbine) is usually radially inward / axialflow in a centrifugal pump is radially outward
output: power; input: head and flowoutput: head and flow; input: power
Centrifugal pump: definition, main parts and working (2021 3b, 2023 3b, 2019 7c)

Pump: a mechanical device that raises the energy (pressure) of a liquid using mechanical energy, to move it from a low level or pressure to a high one. Centrifugal pump: a rotodynamic pump in which the energy is added by the centrifugal action of a rotating impeller; it is the reverse of a radially inward-flow reaction turbine.

PartFunction
Impellerrotating wheel with backward-curved vanes, fixed on the shaft; gives the liquid its velocity and pressure. Types: closed (shrouds on both sides, clean water), semi-open (one shroud, liquids with some solids), open (no shrouds, sewage, paper pulp)
Casingair-tight passage around the impeller; collects the liquid and converts its kinetic energy into pressure energy (volute, vortex, or with guide blades)
Suction pipe with foot valve and strainerconnects the sump to the eye of the impeller; the strainer keeps out debris; the foot valve (one-way) holds the water in the pipe when the pump stops, which helps priming
Delivery pipe with delivery valvecarries the liquid from the casing outlet to the delivery point; the valve controls the flow
Shaft, bearings, couplingtransmit the motor torque to the impeller and keep it aligned
Stuffing box / mechanical seal, wearing ringsstop leakage where the shaft passes through the casing and between impeller and casing

Working (single-stage): (1) The pump is primed: suction pipe, casing and impeller are filled with the liquid so that no air is present. (2) The delivery valve is kept closed and the motor is started; the impeller rotates and creates a forced vortex, which raises the pressure at the outlet and lowers it at the eye. (3) The delivery valve is opened. The low pressure at the eye lets atmospheric pressure push liquid up the suction pipe into the eye. (4) The vanes throw the liquid radially outward at high velocity and pressure. (5) In the casing the area grows, so the velocity falls and the pressure rises further; the liquid leaves through the delivery pipe. The flow is continuous and steady as long as the impeller turns.

Casing with guide blades (2022 3c)

In this casing the impeller is surrounded by a ring of fixed guide blades (vanes) mounted on a diffuser ring. The blade angles match the direction of the liquid leaving the impeller, so the liquid enters the guide passages without shock. The passages between the blades widen gradually, so the velocity falls and the pressure rises; the liquid then passes into the surrounding casing (usually concentric) and to the delivery pipe. Because the conversion of kinetic energy to pressure is gradual and shock-free, efficiency is high; this casing is used in multistage pumps (the guide passages lead the liquid to the eye of the next impeller). The other casings: volute (spiral casing whose area increases steadily to the outlet: simple, but eddies reduce efficiency) and vortex (a circular whirlpool chamber between impeller and volute where a free vortex forms, improving efficiency).

Heads and efficiencies (2021 3c, 2022 3b, 2019 7a)
TermDefinition / formula
Static suction head hsvertical height of the pump centre line above the liquid surface in the sump (suction lift). If the liquid is above the pump it is a positive static suction head
Static delivery head hdvertical height of the liquid surface in the delivery tank (or outlet) above the pump centre line
Static head HsHs = hs + hd: vertical height between the sump and the delivery liquid surfaces
Manometric head Hmhead against which a centrifugal pump has to work: Hm = hs + hd + hfs + hfd + Vd2/2g = (total head at outlet) − (total head at inlet) = Vw2u2/g − losses in the impeller and casing
Manometric efficiency ηmanmanometric head / head imparted by the impeller = gHm/(Vw2u2)
Mechanical efficiency ηmpower delivered by the impeller to the liquid / power input at the shaft = (W/g)Vw2u2/(1000 S.P.)
Overall (pump) efficiency ηowater power / shaft power = ρgQHm/S.P. = ηman × ηm
Water horsepower (WHP)power actually given to the liquid: WHP (water horsepower) = ρgQH/746 (SI, hp) = QH/3960 (Q in gpm, H in ft)
Brake horsepower (BHP)power supplied to the pump shaft: BHP (brake horsepower) = WHP/ηo
Work done by the impeller per second per unit weight (2023 3c)

Assumptions: liquid enters the impeller eye radially (α = 90°, Vw1 = 0, V1 = Vf1); no shock at entry; uniform velocity over the vane passage; no losses. Symbols: N rpm, D1, D2 inlet/outlet diameters, u = πDN/60 vane (tangential) velocity, V absolute velocity, Vw whirl (tangential) component, Vf flow (radial) component, Vr relative velocity.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Mass flow = ρQ kg/s; angular momentum per second at inlet = ρQVw1r1, at outlet = ρQVw2r2Moment of momentum.
Torque on the liquid T = rate of change of angular momentum = ρQ(Vw2r2 − Vw1r1)Newton’s second law for rotation.
Work done per second = Tω = ρQ(Vw2r2ω − Vw1r1ω) = ρQ(Vw2u2 − Vw1u1)u = rω.
Weight of liquid per second = ρgQDivide to get work per unit weight.
Work done per unit weight = (1/g)(Vw2u2 − Vw1u1)Euler’s head (general).
= Vw2u2/g (radial entry, Vw1 = 0)Work done per second = (W/g)Vw2u2, W = ρgQ.

Also Q = πD1B1Vf1 = πD2B2Vf2 (B = vane width). From the velocity triangles, Vw2u2 = (V22 + u22 − Vr22)/2, which gives the fundamental equation: work/unit weight = (V22 − V12)/2g + (u22 − u12)/2g + (Vr12 − Vr22)/2g = rise in kinetic head + rise in pressure head from centrifugal action + from the slowing of relative velocity.

Memory trick: Pump work = “whirl times wheel over g”: Vw2u2/g. Efficiency chain: manometric (hydraulic) × mechanical = overall.

★ REMEMBER IT
  • Re = ρVD/μ: below 2300 laminar (smooth layers), 2300–4000 transitional, above 4000 turbulent (eddies).
  • Major loss = wall friction along the pipe, hf = f(L/D)(V²/2g) (Darcy-Weisbach). Minor losses = fittings: entry, exit, bends, valves, sudden expansion/contraction, h = KV²/2g.
  • Laminar: parabolic profile u = 2Vavg(1 − r²/R²), so umax = 2Vavg and f = 64/Re. Entrance length: laminar ≈ 0.05Re D; turbulent ≈ 10D.
Before you start: what pipe flow is about

A pipe carries a fluid from one place to another. Because the fluid sticks to the wall (the no-slip condition), the velocity is zero at the wall and largest at the centre. The friction this causes uses up energy, which shows up as a fall in pressure along the pipe. We measure that lost energy as a head loss h (metres of the fluid): energy lost per unit weight of fluid.

Three quantities run the whole topic: the Reynolds number Re = ρVD/μ (decides laminar or turbulent), the friction factor f (how rough the flow is), and the head loss hf = f(L/D)(V2/2g).

Laminar and turbulent flow (2020 1a), and how the regions depend on Re (2022 1a)
Laminar flowTurbulent flow
Motionfluid moves in smooth parallel layers (laminae); no mixing between layersfluid particles move in irregular paths with eddies; strong mixing across the pipe
Reynolds number (pipe)Re < 2300Re > 4000 (2300-4000 is transitional: flow switches between the two)
Velocity profileparabolic, umax = 2Vavgflat (full) in the core, very steep near the wall, umax ≈ 1.2Vavg
Shear stressonly viscous: τ = μ du/dyviscous + turbulent (eddy) stress, much larger
Friction factorf = 64/Re, independent of roughnessf = f(Re, ε/D) from Colebrook equation / Moody chart
Head losshf ∝ Vhf ∝ V1.75 to V2
Exampleoil or honey in a thin tube, blood in capillarieswater in city mains, smoke from a chimney, air in ducts

Reynolds number Re = ρVavgD/μ = VavgD/ν = inertia force / viscous force. When inertia wins (high Re) small disturbances grow into eddies: turbulent. When viscosity wins (low Re) disturbances are damped: laminar. The value at which the flow becomes turbulent is the critical Reynolds number, taken as 2300 for a circular pipe.

Hydraulic diameter Dh = 4Ac/p, where Ac is the flow area and p the wetted perimeter (length of wall touched by the fluid). It lets circular-pipe formulas (Re, f, hf) be used for non-circular ducts. Circle: Dh = 4(πD2/4)/(πD) = D. Square of side a: Dh = a. Rectangle a × b: 2ab/(a + b). Annulus: Do − Di.

Entrance region, fully developed flow and the irrotational core (2019 2a(i), 2023 6a, 2022 1a)
  • Irrotational (core) flow region: near the inlet, the central part of the flow outside the boundary layer. Viscous effects are negligible there, the velocity is uniform across the radius and the fluid particles do not rotate.
  • Hydrodynamic entrance region: the length from the pipe inlet to where the velocity profile becomes fully developed. The boundary layer grows from the wall until it meets at the centre; the core accelerates (to keep the mass flow) and the profile keeps changing. Its length Lh ≈ 0.05 Re D for laminar flow and ≈ 10D for turbulent flow. Wall shear (and f) is highest at the inlet and falls along it.
  • Hydrodynamically fully developed region: beyond the entrance length, the velocity profile no longer changes in the flow direction (du/dx = 0). The profile is parabolic in laminar flow and flatter in turbulent flow; the wall shear stress and f are constant, so the pressure falls linearly.
  • How the regions differ with Re: at higher Re the boundary layer grows more slowly relative to D, so the laminar entrance region is longer (Lh ∝ Re); in turbulent flow the mixing makes the entrance short and nearly independent of Re. The fully developed profile is parabolic for Re < 2300 and flat for Re > 4000.
Losses in pipe flow (2021 1a, 2022 1b, 2023 6c, 2019 2a(ii))

Major loss is the loss of head due to friction along a straight pipe of constant area: hf = f(L/D)(V2/2g) (Darcy-Weisbach). Minor losses are losses due to a change in the magnitude or direction of the velocity at fittings; they are written hm = KLV2/2g with a loss coefficient KL found by experiment.

Minor lossHead loss (Bansal)Note
Sudden enlargement(V1 − V2)2/2geddies in the corner after the step
Sudden contraction0.5V22/2g (Cc = 0.62)loss is mostly from the expansion after the vena contracta
Entrance of a pipe0.5V2/2g (sharp edge)rounded entrance: about 0.03
Exit of a pipeV2/2gall kinetic energy is lost in the tank
Obstruction[A/(Cc(A − a)) − 1]2V2/2gpartly closed valve, orifice
Bend, elbow, fittingskV2/2gk from tables (90° elbow about 0.3-0.9)
Major lossMinor loss
due to wall friction along the pipe lengthdue to sudden change of velocity (size or direction) at fittings
hf = fLV2/(2gD), grows with lengthhm = KV2/2g, does not depend on length

Colebrook equation (turbulent): 1/√f = −2.0 log[(ε/D)/3.7 + 2.51/(Re√f)]. It is implicit, so either iterate or read f from the Moody chart, which plots it against Re for each relative roughness ε/D.

Derivation: loss of head due to friction (Darcy-Weisbach) (2020 1a, 2022 1b)

Take a horizontal pipe of diameter D with steady uniform flow V between sections 1 and 2, length L. Let the frictional resistance per unit wetted area per unit velocity squared be f′ (Froude’s experiments: resistance ∝ V2).

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Bernoulli 1 → 2: p1/ρg + V2/2g + z = p2/ρg + V2/2g + z + hf ⇒ hf = (p1 − p2)/ρgSame V (same area) and same z: the pressure drop is the head loss.
Frictional resistance F = f′ × wetted area × V2 = f′(πDL)V2Resistance acts on the wall area πDL.
Force balance on the fluid (no acceleration): (p1 − p2)(πD2/4) = f′πDLV2Net pressure force = friction force.
p1 − p2 = f′(4L/D)V2
hf = (f′/ρg)(4L/D)V2Divide by ρg.
Put f′/ρ = f/8 (Darcy f) or f′/ρ = fF/2 (Fanning fF = f/4)Definition of the friction factor.
hf = f(L/D)(V2/2g) = 4fFLV2/(2gD)Darcy-Weisbach equation.

Side note: Bansal writes hf = 4fLV2/(2gD) where his f is the Fanning (coefficient of friction) = fDarcy/4. Cengel and the lecture use the Darcy f with f = 64/Re for laminar flow. Write one, and say which f it is.

Bernoulli’s equation from Euler’s equation (2021 1b)

Statement: in steady, ideal (non-viscous), incompressible, irrotational flow, the total energy per unit weight is the same at every point on a streamline: p/ρg + V2/2g + z = constant (pressure head + velocity head + datum head). Assumptions: ideal fluid, steady, incompressible, irrotational, along one streamline. For real fluids add the loss: p1/ρg + V12/2g + z1 = p2/ρg + V22/2g + z2 + hL.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Element of area dA, length ds along a streamline; forces: pressure pdA − (p + dp)dA = −dp dA; weight component −ρg dA ds cosθθ = angle between the streamline and the vertical, so ds cosθ = dz.
Mass × acceleration = ρdA ds × V dV/ds (steady flow: as = V dV/ds)Newton’s second law along the streamline.
−dp dA − ρg dA dz = ρ dA V dVSubstitute ds cosθ = dz.
dp/ρ + g dz + V dV = 0Euler’s equation of motion.
Integrate (ρ constant): p/ρ + gz + V2/2 = constantIncompressible.
p/ρg + V2/2g + z = constantBernoulli’s equation, divide by g.
Turbine flow meter (2019 2a(iii))

A multi-bladed rotor is mounted on bearings along the pipe axis. The fluid strikes the angled blades and spins the rotor at a speed proportional to the fluid velocity. A magnetic (or Hall-effect) pick-up outside the pipe produces one pulse each time a blade passes; the pulse frequency f is proportional to the volumetric flow rate, Q = Kf (K = meter factor from calibration). Counting pulses gives the total volume. Accurate (±0.5%), used for fuels, LNG, water meters; needs clean fluid and straight pipe upstream.

Velocity profile of fully developed laminar flow (2019 1c, 2023 6b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Ring element: radius r, thickness dr, length dx. Fully developed, steady: no acceleration, so the net force is zeroOnly pressure and viscous shear act (horizontal pipe).
(2πr dr P)x − (2πr dr P)x+dx + (2πr dx τ)r+dr − (2πr dx τ)r = 0Pressure on the two ends, shear on the outer and inner faces.
Divide by 2πdr dx: r(Px+dx − Px)/dx = [(rτ)r+dr − (rτ)r]/drLet dx, dr → 0.
r dP/dx = d(rτ)/dr, with τ = −μ du/dru falls as r grows, so du/dr < 0 and τ is positive.
(μ/r) d/dr(r du/dr) = dP/dxLeft side depends only on r, right side only on x: both must be the same constant.
Integrate once: r du/dr = (1/2μ)(dP/dx)r2 + C1dP/dx is a constant.
du/dr = (r/2μ)(dP/dx) + C1/r; integrate again: u = (r2/4μ)(dP/dx) + C1ln r + C2

Useful results from the same analysis: ΔP = 8μLVavg/R2 = 32μLVavg/D2; writing ΔP = f(L/D)ρV2/2 gives f = 64/Re; flow rate V̇ = πD4ΔP/(128μL) (Hagen-Poiseuille).

Memory trick: Laminar profile: “two-V, one-minus-r-squared”. The four steps of the proof: balance, separate (both sides constant), integrate twice, two boundary conditions (centre flat, wall zero).

UNDERSTAND Read this to understand; you do not need to write it

Dimensional analysis lets you find the form of a law without solving it. Write every quantity in M, L, T. Buckingham π: n variables and m basic dimensions give (n − m) dimensionless groups. Pick m repeating variables (usually ρ, V, D: one fluid property, one flow, one geometry) and combine each remaining variable with them to make a π group. Pipe friction always ends as ΔP/(ρV²) = φ(Re, L/D, ε/D).

Before you start: why dimensional analysis

Every physical quantity has dimensions built from a few fundamental ones: mass M, length L, time T (and temperature θ). Velocity = LT−1, force = MLT−2, pressure = ML−1T−2, density = ML−3, dynamic viscosity μ = ML−1T−1, kinematic viscosity ν = L2T−1.

Dimensional analysis groups many variables into a few dimensionless numbers. That cuts the number of experiments and lets a small model predict a full-size machine.

Qualitative description of a physical quantity (2019 1a)

A physical quantity is described in two ways. The qualitative description gives its dimension, i.e. what kind of quantity it is, without a number: e.g. length L, mass M, time T, velocity LT−1. The quantitative description gives its size as a number with a unit, e.g. 5 m, 3 m/s. Primary (fundamental) dimensions are M, L, T, θ, current I, amount of light C, amount of matter N; all others are secondary dimensions formed from them.

Dimensional homogeneity (2022 2a)

An equation is dimensionally homogeneous when every additive term has the same dimensions (law of dimensional homogeneity). Such an equation is valid in any system of units, and it can be checked or made non-dimensional by dividing by any one term.

Example: Bernoulli p/ρg + V2/2g + z = H. [p/ρg] = (ML−1T−2)/(ML−3 · LT−2) = L; [V2/2g] = L2T−2/LT−2 = L; [z] = L. Every term is a length (head), so it is homogeneous. Another: V = √(2gH): [V] = LT−1 and [√(gH)] = √(LT−2L) = LT−1.

Buckingham π theorem and Rayleigh’s method (2021 2a, 2023 5a)

Statement: if a physical phenomenon depends on n variables and these involve m fundamental dimensions, the variables can be arranged into (n − m) independent dimensionless groups called π terms: f(X1, ..., Xn) = 0 becomes φ(π1, ..., πn−m) = 0.

  1. List all n variables and write their dimensions; find m.
  2. Pick m repeating variables: together they must contain all m dimensions, must not form a dimensionless group, and should be one geometric (D), one flow (V) and one fluid property (ρ). Never pick the dependent variable.
  3. Each π = (repeating variables with unknown powers) × one remaining variable; set the powers of M, L, T to zero and solve.
  4. Write π1 = φ(π2, π3, ...) and rearrange.
Rayleigh’s methodBuckingham π method
assumes X = K · X1aX2bX3c... and matches powers of M, L, Tgroups variables into (n − m) π terms using repeating variables
gives one equation in all the variablesgives a set of independent dimensionless groups
becomes awkward when there are more than 3-4 independent variables (more unknown powers than equations)systematic for any number of variables
the form of the function is assumed (a product of powers)no form is assumed; the function φ must come from experiment

VariableτwVερμD
DimensionML−1T−2LT−1LML−3ML−1T−1L

π1 = τwVaρbDc: M: 1 + b = 0; T: −2 − a = 0; L: −1 + a − 3b + c = 0 ⇒ a = −2, b = −1, c = 0π1 = τw/(ρV2).
π2 = μVaρbDc: M: 1 + b = 0; T: −1 − a = 0; L: −1 + a − 3b + c = 0 ⇒ a = −1, b = −1, c = −1π2 = μ/(ρVD) = 1/Re.

ΔP = f(D, l, V, ν, ρ, k): n = 7, m = 3, so 4 π terms. Repeating: D, V, ρ.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
π1 = DaVbρcΔP: M: c + 1 = 0; T: −b − 2 = 0; L: a + b − 3c − 1 = 0 ⇒ c = −1, b = −2, a = 0π1 = ΔP/(ρV2).
π2 = DaVbρcl ⇒ a = −1, b = c = 0π2 = l/D.
π3 = DaVbρcν: M: c = 0; T: −b − 1 = 0; L: a + b + 2 = 0 ⇒ b = −1, a = −1π3 = ν/(VD) = 1/Re.
π4 = DaVbρck ⇒ a = −1π4 = k/D.

Memory trick: Repeating variables are “D-V-ρ” (Diameter, Velocity, rho): one for size, one for motion, one for fluid. Each π then reads like a famous number.

★ REMEMBER IT
  • Fan < blower < compressor by pressure ratio: fan up to 1.1, blower 1.1–1.2, compressor above 1.2. Forced draft fan pushes air into the furnace (positive pressure); induced draft fan pulls gases out at the chimney (negative pressure).
Before you start: machines that move gases

Fans, blowers and compressors all raise the pressure of a gas; they differ in how much. A small rise moves air (ventilation); a large rise stores energy in compressed air.

Two ways to raise pressure: squeeze a trapped volume (positive displacement) or give the gas speed and then slow it down (dynamic).

Fan vs blower vs compressor (2020 3a, 2022 3d, 2019 6a)
ItemFanBlowerCompressor
Specific ratio (pdischarge/psuction, ASME)up to 1.111.11 to 1.20above 1.20
Pressure riseup to about 1136 mm WC1136-2066 mm WCabove 2066 mm WC (several bar to hundreds of bar)
Gas density changenegligible (incompressible)smalllarge (compressible); needs cooling/intercooling
Flowvery large volume, low pressuremediumsmaller volume, high pressure
Examplesventilation, cooling towers, FD (forced draught)/ID fans, HVACfurnace air, pneumatic conveying, aeration, cleaningcompressed air plants, refrigeration, gas pipelines, gas turbines
Purpose of a compressor; centrifugal and reciprocating compressors (2023 2c, 2019 6b)

A compressor increases the pressure of a gas by reducing its volume. Purposes: compressed air for pneumatic tools, drills, paint spraying and instrument/control systems; refrigeration and air-conditioning (raises refrigerant vapour pressure); gas turbines and jet engines (combustion air); transport of natural gas in pipelines; supercharging engines; liquefaction and storage of gases; chemical processes that need high pressure and temperature.

Centrifugal compressor (dynamic): gas enters the eye of a high-speed impeller axially; the radial vanes throw it outward, increasing its velocity (and some pressure). It then enters the diffuser, a passage of increasing area where the velocity falls and the kinetic energy changes into pressure; the volute collects the gas and continues the conversion to the outlet. Pressure ratio per stage about 2-4; several stages in series for higher ratios. Smooth, pulsation-free, high flow, compact, little maintenance; less efficient at small flows and subject to surge.

Reciprocating compressor (positive displacement): a piston moves in a cylinder driven by crank and connecting rod. Suction stroke: piston moves down, cylinder pressure falls below suction pressure, the spring-loaded suction valve opens and gas fills the cylinder. Compression stroke: both valves closed, the piston moves up and the gas is compressed (polytropically, pVn = C). Delivery: when the pressure exceeds the delivery pressure the discharge valve opens and gas is pushed out; the gas left in the clearance volume re-expands on the next suction stroke. Single- or double-acting, single- or multi-stage with intercoolers between stages. High pressure ratios, any flow size, but pulsating flow, heavy foundation and more maintenance.

Forced draft vs induced draft fans (2019 8d)
Forced draft (FD) fanInduced draft (ID) fan
placed at the bottom/inlet of the furnace, before the air preheaterplaced at the outlet, between the boiler (dust collector) and the chimney
pushes (forces) fresh air into the furnacesucks (induces) flue gases out of the furnace
furnace pressure above atmospheric (risk of gas leakage out)furnace pressure below atmospheric (air leaks in)
handles cold, clean air: smaller, cheaper, less powerhandles hot, dusty, larger volume of gas: bigger fan, more power, erosion
better flame distribution and air controldraft does not depend on the chimney height

Memory trick: “1.11, 1.20”: fan below 1.11, blower up to 1.20, compressor beyond. FD = “Forces air in”, ID (induced draught (or inside diameter)) = “Inhales gas out”.

Before you start: the recipe for every pipe numerical

1. Find Re = ρVD/μ. 2. Choose f: f = 64/Re if Re < 2300, else Moody chart/Colebrook. 3. Head loss hL = f(L/D)V2/2g. 4. Pressure drop ΔP = ρghL. 5. Pumping power W = V̇ΔP = ρgV̇hL, where V̇ = (πD2/4)V.

Always convert cm and mm to metres first. The diameters in these questions are tiny (2-3 mm), which is why the flow is laminar even for water.

Given: ρ = 1000 kg/m3, μ = 1.519×10−3 kg/m s, D = 0.003 m, L = 9 m, V = 0.9 m/s. Find: hL, ΔP, Ẇ.

Re = ρVD/μ = 1000(0.9)(0.003)/1.519×10−3 = 1777 < 2300Laminar, so f = 64/Re can be used.
f = 64/1777 = 0.0360
hL = f(L/D)V2/2g = 0.0360 × (9/0.003) × 0.92/(2 × 9.81) = 4.46 mHead loss.
ΔP = ρghL = 1000(9.81)(4.46) = 43.7 kPaCheck: 32μLV/D2 = 32(1.519×10−3)(9)(0.9)/0.0032 = 43,747 Pa.
V̇ = (π/4)(0.003)2(0.9) = 6.36×10−6 m3/s
Ẇ = V̇ΔP = 6.36×10−6 × 43,747 = 0.28 WCengel Example 8-2.

Before you start: the LMTD (log mean temperature difference) recipe

1. Energy balance for the unknown flow or outlet temperature. 2. ΔT1, ΔT2 at the two ends. 3. ΔTlm. 4. A = Q/(UΔTlm). 5. L = A/(πD).

Where cp of water is not given, use 4.18 kJ/kg K (Cengel).

★ REMEMBER IT
  • Counter flow beats parallel flow: the cold fluid can leave hotter than the hot fluid's outlet, and ΔT stays more even along the length, so the same Q needs less area.
  • Fouling factor Rf = 1/Udirty − 1/Uclean: scale, rust, deposits add resistance in series. Overall: 1/U = 1/hi + Rf + wall + 1/ho (thin wall).
  • LMTD = (ΔT1 − ΔT2)/ln(ΔT1/ΔT2). Parallel: ΔT1 = Th,in − Tc,in, ΔT2 = Th,out − Tc,out. Counter: ΔT1 = Th,in − Tc,out, ΔT2 = Th,out − Tc,in.
Before you start: the job of a heat exchanger

A heat exchanger moves heat from a hot fluid to a cold fluid, usually through a metal wall so the fluids do not mix: car radiators, condensers, evaporators, oil coolers, boiler economisers. The heat flow is Q = UAΔT, but ΔT changes along the exchanger, so we use the proper mean: the log mean temperature difference.

C = ṁcp (W/K) is the heat capacity rate: how many watts a stream absorbs per degree of temperature change.

Definition, heat exchange and applications, classification (2021 8a, 2022 7a, 2023 7a)

Heat exchanger: a device that transfers heat between two (or more) fluids at different temperatures, usually separated by a solid wall so that they do not mix. Heat exchange is this transfer of thermal energy from the hotter to the colder fluid, by convection on each side and conduction through the wall (radiation in furnaces). Applications: radiators and air-conditioning coils, refrigerator condensers and evaporators, boiler economisers, superheaters and air preheaters, steam power plant condensers, oil coolers in engines and turbines, milk pasteurisers and chillers, chemical and petroleum process heaters, solar water heaters, waste-heat recovery.

BasisTypes
Nature of heat exchangerecuperator (transfer type: fluids separated by a wall, e.g. shell-and-tube); regenerator (storage type: hot and cold fluids flow alternately over a matrix that stores heat, e.g. Ljungström air preheater); direct contact (fluids mix, e.g. cooling tower, jet condenser, open feed-water heater)
Flow arrangementparallel flow (both enter at the same end and flow the same way); counter flow (opposite directions); cross flow (at right angles, mixed or unmixed); multipass (shell-and-tube with several tube passes)
Constructiondouble pipe (concentric tube); shell-and-tube; plate (gasketed plates); plate-fin and tube-fin; regenerative
Compactnesscompact (area density > 700 m2/m3, e.g. car radiator) and non-compact
Phase change / servicecondensers, evaporators, boilers, coolers, heaters
Temperature profiles; why counter flow is more effective (2019 4a, 2023 8a)

In parallel flow the temperature difference is very large at the inlet and becomes small at the outlet; the cold outlet can never be hotter than the hot outlet (both approach the same temperature). In counter flow the hot inlet meets the cold outlet, so ΔT is more nearly uniform along the length, and the cold fluid can leave hotter than the hot fluid leaves.

  1. For the same inlet temperatures, the counter-flow LMTD is larger, so for the same U and A more heat is transferred (or less area is needed for the same duty).
  2. The cold fluid can be heated to nearly the hot inlet temperature (Tc,o > Th,o possible), which is impossible in parallel flow.
  3. The more uniform ΔT means less thermal stress and less entropy generation (less irreversibility).
  4. For the same NTU (number of transfer units) and Cr, εcounter > εparallel; parallel flow has ε ≤ 1/(1 + Cr) (only 0.5 for equal C) while counter flow tends to 1 (see B6).
Fouling factor (2020 5a, 2022 7a)

Fouling is the deposit of unwanted material (scale from hard water, rust, sludge, oil films, biological growth, soot) on heat transfer surfaces during operation. The deposit has low thermal conductivity, so it adds a thermal resistance and reduces the heat transfer (and raises the pressure drop). The fouling factor Rf (m2K/W) is the measure of this extra resistance: Rf = 1/Udirty − 1/Uclean. Typical values: 0.0001 (clean water below 50 °C) to 0.0009 m2K/W (fuel oil, river water). It depends on fluid, temperature, velocity and time; designers add it to size an exchanger that still works after fouling, and cleaning is scheduled when U falls too far.

Overall heat transfer coefficient with fouling (2022 8c) and for a double-pipe exchanger (2021 8b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Heat passes in series: inside convection → inside fouling → wall conduction → outside fouling → outside convectionSame Q through each.
Rconv,i = 1/hiAi; Rf,i/Ai; Rwall = ln(Do/Di)/2πkL; Rf,o/Ao; Rconv,o = 1/hoAoAi = πDiL, Ao = πDoL.
Q = (Th − Tc)/Rtotal = UAΔT ⇒ 1/UA = RtotalDefinition of U.
1/UAs = 1/UiAi = 1/UoAo = 1/hiAi + Rf,i/Ai + ln(Do/Di)/2πkL + Rf,o/Ao + 1/hoAoWith fouling (2022 8c).
Clean, thin, highly conducting wall: Rf = 0, ln term ≈ 0, Ai ≈ Ao = ADouble-pipe tube.
1/U = 1/hi + 1/ho ⇒ U = 1/(1/hi + 1/ho)2021 8b. U is always less than the smaller h.

Effectiveness (2021 8b): ε = actual heat transfer/maximum possible heat transfer = Q/[Cmin(Th,i − Tc,i)] (see B6).

Q = UAΔTlm for parallel flow (2021 7a)

Assumptions: steady flow, no heat loss to the surroundings, constant U and specific heats, negligible kinetic/potential energy changes and axial conduction.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Element dA: dQ = −ṁhcphdTh = ṁccpcdTcHot cools, cold warms, both along x.
dTh = −dQ/Ch, dTc = dQ/Cc ⇒ d(Th − Tc) = −dQ(1/Ch + 1/Cc)
dQ = U(Th − Tc)dA ⇒ d(Th − Tc)/(Th − Tc) = −U dA(1/Ch + 1/Cc)Rate equation.
Integrate inlet (1) to outlet (2): ln(ΔT2/ΔT1) = −UAs(1/Ch + 1/Cc)ΔT1 = Th,i − Tc,i, ΔT2 = Th,o − Tc,o.
Overall balance: 1/Ch = (Th,i − Th,o)/Q, 1/Cc = (Tc,o − Tc,i)/QQ = ChΔTh = CcΔTc.
ln(ΔT2/ΔT1) = −(UAs/Q)[(Th,i − Tc,i) − (Th,o − Tc,o)] = −(UAs/Q)(ΔT1 − ΔT2)Add the two.
Q = UAsΔTlm, ΔTlm = (ΔT1 − ΔT2)/ln(ΔT1/ΔT2)Log mean temperature difference.
LMTD for counter flow; Q = UAΔTlm (2022 7b, 2019 4b, 2023 7b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Take x from the hot inlet. Both fluids’ temperatures fall along x (the cold fluid flows the other way): dQ = −ChdTh = −CcdTcSign of dTc changes compared with parallel flow.
d(Th − Tc) = −dQ(1/Ch − 1/Cc)
With dQ = U(Th − Tc)dA: d(ΔT)/ΔT = −U dA(1/Ch − 1/Cc)
Integrate: ln(ΔT2/ΔT1) = −UAs(1/Ch − 1/Cc)ΔT1 = Th,i − Tc,o (x = 0), ΔT2 = Th,o − Tc,i (x = L).
1/Ch − 1/Cc = [(Th,i − Th,o) − (Tc,o − Tc,i)]/Q = (ΔT1 − ΔT2)/QRearranging the four temperatures.
Q = UAs(ΔT1 − ΔT2)/ln(ΔT1/ΔT2)Same form; only the end ΔTs differ.
If Ch = Cc: ΔT is constant and ΔTlm = ΔT1 = ΔT2Special case.

Memory trick: “Ends, not middles”: ΔT1 and ΔT2 are the hot-minus-cold differences at the two physical ends. Parallel: in-in and out-out. Counter: hot-in minus cold-out, hot-out minus cold-in.

LEARN IT FROM ZERO
Compressible flow, from zero

Below about Mach 0.3 air behaves like water: density stays nearly constant. Faster than that the gas squeezes noticeably, so density, temperature and pressure all change together and the ordinary Bernoulli equation fails.

The key speed is the speed of sound c = √(kRT), the speed at which a small pressure wave travels. Mach number Ma = V/c: < 1 subsonic, ≈ 1 sonic (transonic 0.8–1.2), > 1 supersonic, > 5 hypersonic.

Stagnation (total) properties are what you would get if you stopped the gas without losses: T0/T = 1 + (k − 1)Ma²/2 and P0/P = (T0/T)k/(k−1). A Pitot tube in a fast gas reads P0.

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: when density is no longer constant

For liquids and slow gases the density hardly changes, so Bernoulli works. When a gas moves fast (above about 100 m/s, Ma > 0.3) its density changes noticeably with pressure and temperature: the flow is compressible, and kinetic energy and enthalpy trade places (fast gas is cold gas).

The key speed is the speed of sound c, the speed at which a small pressure disturbance travels. The Mach number Ma = V/c compares the flow speed with it. Answer source: the teachers’ notes do not cover this unit, so these answers follow Cengel & Cimbala (Fluid Mechanics, ch. 12) and Bansal ch. 15, the books in the syllabus.

Compressible vs incompressible flow (2020 4b, 2021 5a, 2022 5a)

Compressible flow is flow in which the density of the fluid changes appreciably from point to point (Δρ/ρ > about 5%), e.g. gas flow at high speed in nozzles, turbines, jet engines. Incompressible flow has (practically) constant density.

Compressible flowIncompressible flow
ρ varies: ρ = f(p, T)ρ = constant
gases at Ma > 0.3; high-speed flows, nozzles, shocksliquids; gases at Ma < 0.3
energy equation includes enthalpy: h + V2/2 = constant; thermodynamics is coupled to the flowmechanical energy (Bernoulli) is enough; temperature decoupled
continuity ρAV = constantAV = constant
pressure waves travel at finite speed c; shocks and choking can occurpressure signals travel instantly (c → ∞)
Mach number is the key parameterReynolds number is the key parameter
Classification by Mach number and definitions (2022 5a, 2023 1a, 2019 5a)
TermMeaning
Mach number Maratio of the local flow velocity to the local speed of sound: Ma = V/c (square root of inertia force/elastic force)
IncompressibleMa < 0.3: density change below about 5%
Subsonic flowMa < 1: flow slower than sound; disturbances travel upstream
Sonic flowMa = 1: flow velocity equals the speed of sound (e.g. at the throat of a choked nozzle)
Transonic0.8 < Ma < 1.2: both subsonic and supersonic regions present
Supersonic1 < Ma < 5: disturbances cannot travel upstream; Mach cone, shocks
HypersonicMa > 5: strong heating, dissociation of gas
Compressible flowflow with significant density variation (above)
Shock wavea very thin region (a few μm) in a supersonic flow across which pressure, temperature and density rise suddenly and velocity falls; irreversible (see B3)
Speed of sound: c = √(K/ρ) and c = √(γP/ρ) (2023 1c, 2019 5c)

Sound is a weak (infinitesimal) pressure wave travelling through a medium; its speed is the speed of sound c. A piston in a duct gives the gas a small velocity dV; a wave moves into the still gas at speed c. Take a control volume moving with the wave: gas enters at c with P, ρ and leaves at c − dV with P + dP, ρ + dρ.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Mass: ρAc = (ρ + dρ)A(c − dV) ⇒ c dρ − ρ dV = 0 (drop dρdV)dV = c dρ/ρ.
Momentum: PA − (P + dP)A = ρAc[(c − dV) − c] ⇒ dP = ρc dVNet force = mass flow × change of velocity.
Combine: dP = ρc (c dρ/ρ) = c2dρ ⇒ c2 = (∂P/∂ρ)sProcess is isentropic (small, fast, reversible, adiabatic).
Bulk modulus K = ρ dP/dρ ⇒ c = √(K/ρ)2019 5c (any fluid; water: √(2.2×109/1000) = 1483 m/s).
Ideal gas, isentropic: P/ργ = C ⇒ dP/dρ = γCργ−1 = γP/ρDifferentiate.
c = √(γP/ρ) = √(γRT)2023 1c. Air at 300 K: √(1.4 × 287 × 300) = 347 m/s.
Stagnation pressure (2023 1b)

Stagnation (total) pressure P0 is the pressure a moving fluid would reach if it were brought to rest isentropically (adiabatically and without friction), e.g. at the nose of a Pitot tube. Similarly T0 and ρ0.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Steady adiabatic energy equation: h + V2/2 = h0 ⇒ cpT + V2/2 = cpT0No work, no heat.
T0/T = 1 + V2/(2cpT); with cp = kR/(k − 1) and c2 = kRT: T0/T = 1 + (k − 1)Ma2/2
Isentropic: P0/P = (T0/T)k/(k−1)Stagnation is reached isentropically.
P0 = P[1 + (k − 1)Ma2/2]k/(k−1)Stagnation pressure.
Binomial expansion: P0 = P + (ρV2/2)[1 + Ma2/4 + (2 − k)Ma4/24 + ...]Bansal form; the bracket is the compressibility correction.
For Ma → 0: P0 = P + ρV2/2Incompressible (Bernoulli) result.
Bernoulli’s equation for adiabatic compressible flow (2019 5b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Euler’s equation: dp/ρ + V dV + g dz = 0From A1.
Adiabatic (isentropic): p/ρk = C ⇒ ρ = (p/C)1/k
∫dp/ρ = C1/k∫p−1/kdp = C1/kp(k−1)/k k/(k − 1) = [k/(k − 1)]p/ρUse C1/k = p1/k/ρ.
[k/(k − 1)](p/ρg) + V2/2g + z = constantBernoulli for adiabatic flow; isothermal flow would give (p/ρg)ln p instead.
Between two sections: [k/(k − 1)](p1/ρ1g) + V12/2g + z1 = [k/(k − 1)](p2/ρ2g) + V22/2g + z2Used in A4 (air venturi).
Critical properties and ratios (2021 5c)

Critical properties (marked *) are the values of P, T, ρ, V at the section where Ma = 1. The critical ratios compare them with stagnation values: T*/T0 = 2/(k + 1), P*/P0 = [2/(k + 1)]k/(k−1), ρ*/ρ0 = [2/(k + 1)]1/(k−1). For air (k = 1.4): 0.8333, 0.5283, 0.6339. Significance: they fix the throat conditions of a choked nozzle; if the back pressure is below P* = 0.528P0 the flow chokes and the mass flow is maximum; A* is the reference area for A/A* tables; they are used to design nozzles and to check whether flow can become supersonic.

Numerical: velocity with and without compressibility (2021 5d)

Given: P0 = 100 kPa, T0 = 308.15 K, P = 52 kPa, k = 1.4, R = 287 (cp = kR/(k − 1) = 1004.5 J/kg K).

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Compressible: T = T0(P/P0)(k−1)/k = 308.15(0.52)0.2857 = 255.6 KIsentropic from stagnation.
V = √[2cp(T0 − T)] = √[2 × 1004.5 × 52.5] = 324.8 m/sMa = 324.8/√(1.4 × 287 × 255.6) = 1.01.
Ignoring compressibility: ρ = ρ0 = P0/RT0 = 100,000/(287 × 308.15) = 1.131 kg/m3Density fixed at its stagnation value.
P0 − P = ρV2/2 ⇒ V = √[2 × 48,000/1.131] = 291.4 m/sBernoulli.
Error = (324.8 − 291.4)/324.8 = 10%Compressibility matters at this speed.

Side note: If the static density P/RT = 0.709 kg/m3 is used instead, the incompressible answer is 368 m/s; state which density you use.

Memory trick: “c = root kRT”; stagnation: “one plus k-minus-one-over-two Ma squared” for T, raise to k/(k − 1) for P. Air critical: 0.833, 0.528, 0.634.

B3 Shock waves: normal and oblique shocks, Rayleigh line, normal-shock numericals Very likely · 93%Medium

  • 2022 Q6(c) [12] Air, normal shock at Ma = 2.5, upstream 61.64 kPa and 262.15 K: downstream pressure, temperature, velocity, Mach number, stagnation pressure.
  • 2021 Q6(b) [5] Differentiate between normal and oblique shock waves.
  • 2021 Q6(c) [14] Air enters a C-D (converging-diverging) nozzle at 1 MPa, 300 K, low velocity; normal shock at the exit plane at Ma = 2: pressure, temperature, Mach number, velocity after the shock.

UNDERSTAND Read this to understand; you do not need to write it

A normal shock is a very thin jump, square to the flow, where supersonic flow suddenly becomes subsonic. Pressure, temperature and density jump up; velocity and Mach drop; stagnation temperature stays the same (adiabatic) but stagnation pressure drops (it is irreversible, entropy rises). An oblique shock is tilted, turns the flow, and the flow behind it can stay supersonic.

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: what a shock is

Supersonic flow cannot ‘feel’ an obstacle or a high back pressure ahead of it, because pressure signals travel only at the speed of sound. So the flow adjusts suddenly, across a very thin wave: a shock wave. Across it the velocity drops and P, T, ρ jump up. It is irreversible: entropy rises and stagnation pressure falls, but stagnation temperature stays the same (adiabatic).

All normal-shock numericals: (1) Ma2 from Ma1, (2) P2/P1 and T2/T1, (3) V2 = Ma2√(kRT2), (4) P02 = P2[1 + (k − 1)Ma22/2]k/(k−1). Use formulas or the normal-shock table.

Shock wave, normal shock and oblique shock (2022 6a, 2021 6b)
  • Shock wave: an extremely thin region (about 0.1-1 μm) in a supersonic flow across which the flow properties change abruptly: velocity and Mach number fall, pressure, temperature, density and entropy rise; the process is adiabatic and irreversible.
  • Normal shock wave: a shock perpendicular to the flow direction; the flow is always supersonic upstream and subsonic downstream; flow direction does not change. Occurs in C-D nozzles at off-design back pressure, in supersonic inlets, ahead of blunt bodies.
  • Oblique shock wave: a shock inclined at an angle β to the flow, formed when supersonic flow is turned into itself (wedge, compression corner). The flow is deflected by the angle θ; the downstream flow is usually still supersonic (weaker shock).
Normal shockOblique shock
perpendicular to the flow (β = 90°)inclined at β < 90°
no change of flow directionflow turned through angle θ
downstream always subsonic (Ma2 < 1)downstream usually supersonic (only the normal component becomes subsonic)
strongest: largest loss of P0weaker: smaller entropy rise and loss
1-D analysis2-D analysis (θ-β-Ma relation)
Rayleigh line (2023 2a)

The Rayleigh line is the locus of states (on an h-s or T-s diagram) of a frictionless flow in a constant-area duct with heat transfer: all states have the same mass flux and the same momentum flux (P + ρV2). The Fanno line has the same mass flux and the same stagnation enthalpy (adiabatic flow with friction). A normal shock satisfies all three (mass, momentum, energy), so its upstream and downstream states are the two intersections of the Rayleigh and Fanno lines.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Momentum, constant area, no friction: P1 + ρ1V12 = P2 + ρ2V22Rayleigh line condition.
ρV2 = ρMa2c2 = ρMa2(kP/ρ) = kPMa2Ideal gas, c2 = kP/ρ.
P1(1 + kMa12) = P2(1 + kMa22)
P2/P1 = (1 + kMa12)/(1 + kMa22)Equation of the Rayleigh line (also the normal-shock pressure ratio).

Step (write this)Why / what it means

Momentum (above): P2/P1 = (1 + kMa12)/(1 + kMa22)

Equate the two P2/P1: (1 + kMa12)/(1 + kMa22) = (Ma1/Ma2)√{{[1 + (k − 1)Ma12/2]/[1 + (k − 1)Ma22/2]}}One equation in Ma1 and Ma2.
Square and rearrange: Ma12[1 + (k − 1)Ma12/2]/(1 + kMa12)2 = Ma22[1 + (k − 1)Ma22/2]/(1 + kMa22)2Same function of Ma on each side.
This is a quadratic in Ma22; one root is Ma2 = Ma1 (no shock); the other root isDivide out the trivial root.
Ma22 = [Ma12 + 2/(k − 1)] / [2kMa12/(k − 1) − 1]Check: Ma1 = 2, k = 1.4: (4 + 5)/(28 − 1) = 0.333, Ma2 = 0.577.

LEARN IT FROM ZERO
Effectiveness-NTU, from zero

LMTD (log mean temperature difference) needs all four temperatures. When you know only the inlets and the exchanger size, use ε-NTU instead.

  • Heat capacity rates C = ṁcp for each fluid; Cmin is the smaller, c = Cmin/Cmax.
  • Qmax = Cmin(Th,in − Tc,in): the most heat any exchanger could pass (infinitely long counter flow).
  • Effectiveness ε = Q/Qmax.
  • NTU = UA/Cmin: the "size" of the exchanger. Bigger NTU, higher ε, with diminishing returns.

Parallel flow: ε = [1 − e−NTU(1+c)]/(1 + c). Counter flow: ε = [1 − e−NTU(1−c)]/[1 − c e−NTU(1−c)]. Then Q = εQmax and the outlets follow.

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Interactive graph (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: why a second method

LMTD is easy when all four temperatures are known (design/sizing problem). When an exchanger already exists (area known) and the outlet temperatures are unknown (rating problem), LMTD needs trial and error. The effectiveness-NTU method solves it directly.

Three numbers: Cr = Cmin/Cmax, NTU = UA/Cmin (the ‘size’ of the exchanger), and ε = Q/Qmax (how good it is).

Effectiveness and its significance (2022 8a, 2021 8b)

Effectiveness ε = actual heat transfer rate / maximum possible heat transfer rate = Q/Qmax, with Qmax = Cmin(Th,i − Tc,i): the heat that would be transferred in an infinitely long counter-flow exchanger, where the fluid with the smaller C would undergo the full temperature difference. Significance: 0 ≤ ε ≤ 1 measures the thermal performance; once ε is known, Q = εCmin(Th,i − Tc,i) and both outlet temperatures follow without iteration; it allows comparison of different exchanger types and flow arrangements.

Physical significance of NTU (2021 7b)

NTU = UAs/Cmin (number of transfer units) is a dimensionless measure of the heat transfer size of the exchanger: the ratio of the exchanger’s heat transfer conductance UA to the heat capacity rate of the weaker fluid. Large NTU means a large area (or high U) compared with the flow: the fluid gets close to the limiting temperature and ε is high. Beyond NTU ≈ 3 ε rises very little, so a bigger exchanger is not economical. The method lets outlet temperatures be found directly when the exchanger size is known.

Counter flow has higher effectiveness (2022 8b)

For the same NTU and Cr, εcounter = [1 − e−NTU(1−Cr)]/[1 − Cre−NTU(1−Cr)] is always larger than εparallel = [1 − e−NTU(1+Cr)]/(1 + Cr). Example NTU = 2, Cr = 1: parallel 0.49, counter 0.67. As NTU → ∞ parallel flow is limited to 1/(1 + Cr) because both outlets approach one common temperature, while counter flow approaches 1 because the cold fluid can be heated up to the hot inlet temperature. Physically, the temperature difference stays large over the whole length in counter flow (larger LMTD). (Only when Cr = 0, e.g. a condensing or boiling fluid, are the two equal: ε = 1 − e−NTU.)

Effectiveness of a parallel-flow exchanger (2020 6a, 2023 8b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
From the LMTD derivation (B4): ln[(Th,o − Tc,o)/(Th,i − Tc,i)] = −UAs(1/Ch + 1/Cc)Parallel flow.
Let the cold fluid be Cmin: −(UAs/Cc)(1 + Cc/Ch) = −NTU(1 + Cr)NTU = UAs/Cmin, Cr = Cmin/Cmax. (Same result if hot is Cmin.)
ε = Cc(Tc,o − Tc,i)/[Cmin(Th,i − Tc,i)] ⇒ Tc,o = Tc,i + ε(Th,i − Tc,i)Definition.
Energy balance: Th,o = Th,i − (Cc/Ch)(Tc,o − Tc,i) = Th,i − Crε(Th,i − Tc,i)
Th,o − Tc,o = (Th,i − Tc,i) − ε(1 + Cr)(Th,i − Tc,i)Subtract.
(Th,o − Tc,o)/(Th,i − Tc,i) = 1 − ε(1 + Cr)
ln[1 − ε(1 + Cr)] = −NTU(1 + Cr) ⇒ 1 − ε(1 + Cr) = e−NTU(1+Cr)Combine with the first step.
ε = [1 − e−NTU(1 + Cmin/Cmax)]/(1 + Cmin/Cmax), NTU = UoAo/CminThe required result.

UNDERSTAND Read this to understand; you do not need to write it

dA/A = (Ma² − 1)dV/V explains every nozzle. Subsonic (Ma < 1): to speed up, the area must shrink. Supersonic (Ma > 1): to speed up, the area must grow. So reaching supersonic needs a converging-diverging nozzle with Ma = 1 exactly at the throat. Once the throat is sonic, lowering the back pressure further does not raise the mass flow: the nozzle is choked (P* = 0.528P0 for air).

Interactive graph (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: why a supersonic nozzle must diverge

For a liquid, a narrower pipe always means faster flow. For a gas this is true only while the flow is subsonic. Above Ma = 1 the gas expands (its density falls) faster than the velocity rises, so it needs a bigger area to go faster. A rocket nozzle therefore converges to a throat (Ma = 1) and then diverges.

Use stagnation values (P0, T0) as the reference: they stay constant through an isentropic nozzle.

Area-velocity relation: velocity and area in supersonic flow, and C-D duct as nozzle or diffuser (2020 4a, 2021 5b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Continuity: ρAV = constant ⇒ dρ/ρ + dA/A + dV/V = 0Log-differentiate.
Euler (isentropic, horizontal): dP = −ρV dVMomentum.
dP = c2dρ ⇒ dρ/ρ = dP/(ρc2) = −V dV/c2 = −Ma2dV/VSpeed of sound.
dA/A = −dV/V − dρ/ρ = −dV/V + Ma2dV/VSubstitute.
dA/A = (Ma2 − 1) dV/V   and   dA/A = [(1 − Ma2)/ρV2] dPArea-velocity relation.
CaseSignResult
Ma < 1Ma2 − 1 < 0: dA and dV oppositeconverging (dA < 0) speeds the flow up (nozzle); diverging slows it (diffuser)
Ma > 1Ma2 − 1 > 0: dA and dV same signdiverging (dA > 0) speeds the flow up (nozzle); converging slows it (diffuser). This proves 2020 4a
Ma = 1dA = 0sonic speed can occur only where the area is a minimum: the throat

C-D duct as nozzle or diffuser (2021 5b): subsonic flow entering a converging-diverging duct speeds up in the converging part; if Ma reaches 1 at the throat, it keeps speeding up in the diverging part (supersonic) and the duct is a nozzle (dV > 0 throughout). If instead supersonic flow enters, the converging part slows it to Ma = 1 at the throat and the diverging part slows it further as subsonic flow: the duct is a diffuser (dV < 0 throughout, pressure rises). Which one depends on the inlet Mach number and back pressure; this follows directly from the sign of (Ma2 − 1).

Maximum mass flow rate (2021 6a)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
ṁ = ρAV = (P/RT) A Ma√(kRT) = PAMa√(k/RT)Ideal gas and V = Ma c.
P = P0[1 + (k − 1)Ma2/2]−k/(k−1), T = T0[1 + (k − 1)Ma2/2]−1Isentropic relations.
ṁ = AP0Ma√(k/RT0) / [1 + (k − 1)Ma2/2](k+1)/[2(k−1)]Powers: k/(k − 1) − 1/2 = (k + 1)/[2(k − 1)].
For fixed P0, T0, ṁ/A is largest where A is smallest; setting d(ṁ/A)/dMa = 0 gives Ma = 1Maximum flux at sonic throat.
Put Ma = 1, A = A*: 1 + (k − 1)/2 = (k + 1)/2
ṁmax = A*P0√(k/RT0) [2/(k + 1)](k+1)/[2(k−1)]Air: ṁmax = 0.6847A*P0/√(RT0).
Effect of back pressure on a converging nozzle (2022 5b)
  1. Pb = P0: no flow; pressure is P0 everywhere.
  2. P0 > Pb > P*: subsonic flow throughout; exit pressure Pe = Pb; lowering Pb increases the velocity and the mass flow.
  3. Pb = P* (= 0.528P0 for air): Ma = 1 at the exit; the mass flow reaches its maximum: the nozzle is choked.
  4. Pb < P*: the exit stays at Pe = P*, Mae = 1 and ṁ = ṁmax: lowering Pb further has no effect inside the nozzle because pressure signals cannot travel upstream through the sonic exit. The gas expands from P* to Pb outside the nozzle through expansion waves.

Mass flow can be raised only by increasing P0, lowering T0 or enlarging the throat.

Memory trick: dA/A = (Ma2 − 1)dV/V: “below one, opposite; above one, same”.
